title: Nothing Has Left
passage:
Ask why bread goes stale and the answer comes back that it dries out. The panels at the Ostwick baking institute do not agree, and neither do its scales. A loaf sealed in a bag loses almost no water overnight, and the tasters still mark it down by morning; the crust, meanwhile, which went into the bag crisp, has gone limp. Two changes are running in opposite directions inside one loaf: the crumb stiffens as its starch settles back into an ordered form, and the water it gives up moves outwards and softens the crust. Nothing has left the bag; it has only moved. Cecilia Vanhoof, who runs the sensory panel, likes the awkward consequence best. The oldest freshness test in the trade, a squeeze of the crust, reads a loaf backwards, because the part being squeezed is the part that is getting softer.
— Aurelia Tomczyk, science notebook

questions.rationale: TYPE-004 whole-text gist. The passage opens by naming the common answer (bread dries out), sets both the scales and the tasters against it, and states its own account in the middle: the crumb stiffens while the water it releases moves outwards and softens the crust — 'Nothing has left the bag; it has only moved.' B is that thesis, compressed into its water half: the passage subordinates the starch clause as the cause of the water release ('the water it gives up'), and the summary sentence, the title and the closing consequence are all water-migration claims, so B names the thesis rather than denying the starch mechanism. A = outside_knowledge: keeping a bagged crust crisp is a plausible kitchen concern the passage never raises — the bagged loaf is its test case and the limp crust its evidence, but no method for keeping a crust crisp is offered or even considered anywhere in the text. C = surface_word_match with the disagreement misassigned: the tasters and the scales are on the same side of the argument here — both tell against the drying explanation, the scales by finding almost no water lost and the tasters by marking the loaf down anyway — so no dispute between them exists to be the subject. D = polarity_contrast_miss: the passage says 'Two changes are running in opposite directions' and D runs both of them the wrong way — water inwards instead of outwards, and a crumb that goes on softening instead of one that 'stiffens as its starch settles back into an ordered form' — so it is the option for a student who has registered that something moves between crumb and crust but not which way, and it is the one distractor that dies only on a check against the two clauses that name the direction. Hedge balance: all four options are flat topic statements with no hedges and no absolutes, so the key cannot be found by tone; the key is 15 words against 15 / 14 / 16, so it is joint-second and not the longest. No two options stand in a contradictory relation, so the set cannot be narrowed to a pair on form alone, and B is not the only whole-loaf account on offer.
